title: How We Know: Old Books and Those Who Study Them
bigQuestion: How do old writings, hand-made copies and translations help researchers learn what the Bible's first readers heard?

story.title: The Verse That Stopped Her
story.kicker: A college student reads one short verse in Hebrew and has to read it again.
paragraphs: Nina sat in the college library with a thick book open in front of her. It was a Hebrew Bible. The letters ran from right to left. She had studied Hebrew for one year. Now her teacher had asked the class to read Psalm 82 on their own.

The first verse was short. Nina found the word for God. Then she found the same word again, a few words later. The first time, it meant God. The second time, it seemed to mean many beings. The verse seemed to say that God stands in a council and judges among the gods.

Nina frowned. She checked her dictionary. She checked her grammar notes. The word was elohim both times. The grammar showed that the first one was one being and the second one was many. She raised her hand and asked, "Who are the other elohim?"

Her teacher smiled. "That is a very old question," she said. "Start with the psalm itself. That is your primary source. Then read the scholars. Some compare it with old clay tablets from Syria. Some, like Michael Heiser, say this psalm surprised them too. They do not all agree."

Nina wrote two lists in her notebook. One said Old Writings. The other said Scholars. At the top of the page she wrote her question. She wanted to know what the first people who heard this psalm thought it meant.
story.think: Nina's teacher said to read the psalm itself before reading the scholars. Why might that order help?

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
lessons.mainIdea: A primary source is the old writing itself; a secondary source is what a later scholar writes about it.
reading: In 1947, shepherds found old scrolls hidden in a cave near the Dead Sea. One was a long scroll of the Book of Isaiah, made of animal skin. It was copied by hand more than 2,000 years ago. A scroll like this is a *primary source*. It is the old writing itself.

Other primary sources are clay tablets, carved stones and the books of the Bible. They come from the time being studied, or they are careful copies from long ago. They let a reader see the very words the old writers chose.

A *secondary source* is what a later person writes about an old writing. A scholar's book about Isaiah is a secondary source. It can help a lot. But good researchers always go back and check the primary source first.

words.d: the old writing itself, like a scroll, a clay tablet or a book of the Bible
what a later person, like a scholar, writes about an old writing
a long roll of animal skin or papyrus with writing on it

look.title: Sort the Sources
look.text: 1. The Great Isaiah Scroll from a cave near the Dead Sea. 2. A clay tablet from the old city of Ugarit. 3. A 2015 book by a scholar explaining the Psalms. 4. Psalm 82 in a Hebrew Bible. 5. A teacher's video about the Dead Sea Scrolls.
look.prompt: Which of these are primary sources? Which are secondary sources? Explain one of your choices.

check.q: What is a primary source?
choices: A book a scholar writes today
The old writing itself, like a scroll or tablet
check.why: A primary source is the old writing itself, such as the Great Isaiah Scroll.

check.q: Which of these is a secondary source?
choices: A modern scholar's book about Isaiah
check.why: A scholar's book about Isaiah is written later about the old text, so it is secondary.

check.q: What do good researchers do before trusting what a scholar says?
check.why: The reading says good researchers go back and check the primary source first.

lessons.title: Copies Made by Hand
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible's first writings are lost; what survive are manuscripts, hand-made copies that scholars compare.
reading: Before printing machines, every book was copied by hand. A copy written by hand is called a *manuscript*. The very first writings of the Bible are lost. What survive are manuscripts, copies of copies, made by careful *scribes*.

Some manuscripts are very old. The Great Isaiah Scroll was copied about 125 BCE. Codex Sinaiticus, a Greek Bible, was copied in the 300s CE. The Leningrad Codex, from 1008 CE, is the oldest complete Hebrew Bible that survives.

Scholars lay manuscripts side by side. Most of the time the copies agree closely. Sometimes one word is different. Then scholars ask which reading is older. Later in this course you will see a famous difference in Deuteronomy 32:8.

words.d: a copy of a text written by hand
trained writers who copied texts by hand
an old book with pages sewn together, instead of a scroll

look.title: How Old Are These Copies?
look.cite: Common scholarly dates: Great Isaiah Scroll c. 125 BCE; Codex Sinaiticus c. 350 CE; Leningrad Codex 1008 CE
look.prompt: Which copy is oldest? About how many years older is it than the Leningrad Codex?

check.q: What is a manuscript?
choices: A copy of a text written by hand
check.why: A manuscript is a hand-written copy, made before printing.

check.q: Which manuscript is the oldest complete Hebrew Bible that survives?
check.why: The Leningrad Codex, from 1008 CE, is the oldest complete Hebrew Bible.

check.q: When two copies differ, what do scholars ask?
check.why: Scholars compare manuscripts to find which reading is older.

lessons.title: Clay Tablets From Ugarit
lessons.mainIdea: Clay tablets from the old city of Ugarit are primary sources that show words and ideas Israel's neighbors knew.
reading: In 1928 a farmer in Syria hit a stone while plowing. It led to the ruins of an old city called Ugarit. Beginning in 1929, diggers found thousands of *clay tablets* there. Scribes had pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay, about 3,300 years ago.

Some Ugarit tablets tell stories about their gods. In them, the high god El leads a gathering of gods, called his *assembly*. The gods in it are called the sons of El. Some of the same kinds of words for a heavenly gathering also appear in the Hebrew Bible.

Scholars read these tablets beside the Bible. E. Theodore Mullen (1980) and Mark S. Smith (2001) are two who compared them closely. Many say Bible writers used words their neighbors knew. In the Bible's council scenes, Israel's God is at the head, not El or Baal.

words.d: flat pieces of clay with writing pressed into them while wet
a gathering of members who meet together, like a council
an old city on the coast of Syria whose clay tablets were found starting in 1929

look.title: Two Gatherings Side by Side
look.text: Ugarit tablets: the high god El leads an assembly of gods called the sons of El. Psalm 82 (Hebrew Bible): God stands in a council and judges among the gods.
look.prompt: What is the same in these two pictures? What is different about who is in charge?

check.q: What did diggers find at Ugarit?
check.why: Starting in 1929, diggers found thousands of clay tablets at Ugarit.

check.q: In the Ugarit tablets, who leads the assembly of the gods?
check.why: The tablets show the high god El leading an assembly called the sons of El.

check.q: Why do scholars like Mullen and Smith read Ugarit tablets beside the Bible?
choices: They were written by King David
They show words and ideas Israel's neighbors knew
They are part of the New Testament
check.why: The tablets use council words and ideas that Israel's neighbors knew.

lessons.title: Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible was first written in three languages: mostly Hebrew, a little Aramaic, and Greek for the New Testament.
reading: Most of the Hebrew Bible, or Old Testament, was written in *Hebrew*. Hebrew is written from right to left. Its alphabet has 22 letters, all consonants. Marks for the vowels were added much later by scribes called the Masoretes.

A few parts are in *Aramaic*, a sister language of Hebrew. Parts of Daniel and Ezra are in Aramaic. Later, Aramaic became an everyday language in Israel. Some old pieces of the Book of Enoch, found near the Dead Sea, are in Aramaic too.

The New Testament was written in *Greek*. By then Greek was a shared language around the eastern Mediterranean Sea. So a reader of the whole Bible meets three languages. Scholars who study these texts learn all three.

words.d: the language of most of the Hebrew Bible, written from right to left
a sister language of Hebrew, used in parts of Daniel and Ezra
the language the New Testament was written in

look.title: Letters in Four Alphabets
look.cite: Standard alphabets of Hebrew, Greek, English and Ugaritic
look.prompt: Which alphabet has the most letters? How many more letters does English have than Hebrew?

check.q: In which language was the New Testament written?
check.why: The New Testament books were written in Greek.

check.q: Which books of the Hebrew Bible have parts in Aramaic?
check.why: Parts of Daniel and Ezra are written in Aramaic.

check.q: Which way is Hebrew written?
check.why: Hebrew is written from right to left.

lessons.title: Carrying Words Into English
lessons.mainIdea: A translation carries old words into a new language, and translators must choose how to say each word.
reading: A *translation* carries words from one language into another. In the 200s BCE, Jewish scholars in Alexandria, Egypt, began putting the Hebrew Bible into Greek. This Greek translation is called the *Septuagint*.

Translators must make choices. In Psalm 8:5, the Hebrew says people were made a little lower than elohim. The Septuagint chose the Greek word for angels. The King James Version of 1611 said angels too. Some newer English Bibles say God or heavenly beings instead.

Translations also carry books outside the Bible. The Book of Enoch survived whole in *Ge'ez*, an old language of Ethiopia. R. H. Charles put it into English in 1917. Comparing translations shows where a word could go more than one way.

words.d: words carried from one language into another
the old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in Egypt in the 200s BCE
an old language of Ethiopia in which the whole Book of Enoch survived

look.title: A Little Lower Than the Angels
look.text: For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour.
look.prompt: The Hebrew word behind angels here is elohim. Why might the translators have chosen angels?

check.q: What is the Septuagint?
choices: An old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
check.why: The Septuagint is the Greek translation begun in Alexandria in the 200s BCE.

check.q: In Psalm 8:5, which word does the King James Version use for elohim?
check.why: Following the Septuagint, the KJV says 'a little lower than the angels.'

check.q: In which language did the whole Book of Enoch survive?
check.why: The complete Book of Enoch survived in Ge'ez, an old language of Ethiopia.

lessons.title: One Word, Many Beings
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew word elohim can mean Israel's God, and it is also used for other beings of the spirit world.
reading: Psalm 82:1 is a short verse. It says God stands in a council and judges among the gods. In Hebrew, the word for God and the word for gods are the same word: *elohim*. English Bibles have to pick two different words.

Elohim appears about 2,600 times in the Hebrew Bible. Most of the time it means Israel's God, as in Genesis 1:1. But 1 Kings 11:33 uses it for the god of the *Moabites*. Psalm 82:1 uses it for the beings in God's council.
So one Hebrew word points to many beings. In English, God with a capital G names one being. In Hebrew, elohim is a wider word. Readers use the rest of the sentence to see which being is meant.

words.d: a Hebrew word used for Israel's God and also for other beings of the spirit world
a people who lived east of the Dead Sea, neighbors of ancient Israel

look.title: Two English Words for One Hebrew Word
look.text: God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.
look.prompt: In Hebrew, God and gods are the same word, elohim. Which one means one being? Which means many?

check.q: What can the Hebrew word elohim mean?
choices: Israel's God, and also other spirit beings
check.why: Elohim is used for Israel's God and for other beings of the spirit world.

check.q: In 1 Kings 11:33, elohim is used for whom?
check.why: First Kings 11:33 uses elohim for the god of the Moabites.

check.q: In Psalm 82:1 (KJV), which two English words translate elohim?
check.why: The KJV says God stands and judges among the gods; both words are elohim in Hebrew.

lessons.title: Scholars Explain It Differently
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars explain the word elohim in different ways, and each one points to the text.
reading: Why does elohim fit so many beings? Scholars give different answers. Michael S. Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015), said elohim is a word about *residence*. It tells where a being lives: the spirit world. It does not tell what the being is like.

Heiser compared it to a word like Illinoisan. A baby and a farmer can both be Illinoisans. For him, Israel's God is an elohim, but no other elohim is like him. Exodus 15:11 asks this too: who among the gods is like the LORD?

Other scholars explain elohim in other ways. In Exodus 22:8, the King James Version even says judges for elohim. Mark S. Smith (2001) studied how Israel's writers spoke about God and other gods over time. Readers still discuss the word today.

words.d: the place where someone lives
the unseen world the Bible describes, where God and heavenly beings are said to live
a person who studies one subject very deeply and writes about it

look.title: One Scholar on the Word Elohim
look.text: Heiser explains that elohim is a word for any being whose home is the spirit world. The word tells where a being lives. It does not tell what the being is like or how powerful it is.
look.cite: Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm (Lexham Press, 2015), paraphrased
look.prompt: How is elohim, as Heiser explains it, like the word Illinoisan? How does Exodus 22:8 in the KJV show another way to read it?

check.q: Heiser said the word elohim tells what about a being?
choices: Where its home is: the spirit world
That it is equal to God
check.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser called elohim a word about residence.

check.q: In Exodus 22:8, how does the King James Version translate elohim?
check.why: The KJV says the master of the house is brought to the judges; the Hebrew word is elohim.

check.q: Which verse asks, who among the gods is like the LORD?
check.why: Exodus 15:11, in the song after crossing the sea, asks this question.

lessons.title: One or Many? Context Tells
lessons.mainIdea: Elohim looks plural, but the words around it show whether it means one being or many.
reading: In Hebrew, the ending -im often makes a word *plural*, meaning more than one. Elohim ends in -im. So how can it mean one God? Hebrew readers look at the words around it. When elohim goes with a verb for one person, it means one being.

Genesis 1:1 uses elohim with a verb for one person. So it means one God, who creates. But in Psalm 82:1, the second elohim is in a phrase that needs more than one. God judges in the midst of the elohim. You can only stand in the midst of many.

English has a word like this. The word sheep can mean one sheep or many sheep. You know which one from the sentence. The sheep is eating means one. The sheep are eating means many. Scholars of every view use this kind of *context* clue.

words.d: meaning more than one
the words, time, place and ideas around a text that help explain what it means

look.title: Find the Clue
look.text: Sentence A: The sheep is in the barn. Sentence B: The sheep are in the barn. Psalm 82:1 (retold): God stands in the council; he judges in the midst of the elohim.
look.prompt: Which word in Sentences A and B tells you one or many? In Psalm 82:1, which words tell you the second elohim means many?

check.q: What does the ending -im often do to a Hebrew word?
check.why: The Hebrew ending -im often marks a plural.

check.q: How do readers know elohim means one God in Genesis 1:1?
choices: It goes with a verb for one person
It is in a different book
check.why: In Genesis 1:1 elohim goes with a verb for one person, so it means one God.

check.q: Which English word works like elohim, meaning one or many?
check.why: Sheep can mean one or many; the sentence shows which, as with elohim.

lessons.title: Scholars and the Book of Enoch
lessons.mainIdea: Researchers found, translated and studied the old copies of the Book of Enoch, starting from the manuscripts themselves.
reading: Genesis 5:24 says Enoch walked with God, and then he was gone, because God took him. Much later, other writers told longer stories about Enoch. These were gathered into the Book of Enoch, also called *1 Enoch*.

In the 1950s, pieces of 1 Enoch in Aramaic turned up in caves near Qumran, by the Dead Sea. J. T. Milik published them in 1976. Loren Stuckenbruck studied another scroll from there, the Book of Giants, in 1997. These *fragments* are small, but they show the stories are very old.

George Nickelsburg and James VanderKam made a new English translation of 1 Enoch in 2004. Michael Heiser also wrote about these texts. Each *researcher* starts with the old writing, then explains what it may mean.

words.d: an old Jewish book of stories and visions about Enoch, also called the Book of Enoch
small broken pieces of an old scroll or tablet
a person who studies sources carefully to find out what is true about them

look.title: When the Studies Came Out
rows: R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch
J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch
L. Stuckenbruck, The Book of Giants from Qumran
G. Nickelsburg and J. VanderKam, 1 Enoch
look.cite: Charles (1917); Milik (1976); Stuckenbruck (1997); Nickelsburg and VanderKam (2004); Heiser (2015)
look.prompt: How many years passed between Charles's translation and Nickelsburg and VanderKam's? Why might a new translation help after the Aramaic fragments were found?

check.q: What does Genesis 5:24 say about Enoch?
choices: He found the Dead Sea Scrolls
He walked with God, and God took him
check.why: Genesis 5:24 says Enoch walked with God and was gone, for God took him.

check.q: Who published the Aramaic pieces of 1 Enoch from Qumran in 1976?
check.why: J. T. Milik published the Aramaic fragments of Enoch from Qumran Cave 4 in 1976.

check.q: What did George Nickelsburg and James VanderKam make in 2004?
choices: A new English translation of 1 Enoch
check.why: Nickelsburg and VanderKam published 1 Enoch: A New Translation in 2004.

lessons.title: The First Readers' World
lessons.mainIdea: Researchers try to read an old text the way its first readers would have understood it.
reading: Think of a text message from today. Someone reading it 3,000 years from now might be confused. What is a phone? What does a smiley face mean? They would need to learn about our world first. Old writings are like that too.

The first readers of the Hebrew Bible lived in the *ancient Near East*. That is the name for lands like Israel, Egypt, Syria and Iraq long ago. People there had their own ideas about kings, gods, temples and the sky. Bible writers used words those readers knew.

So researchers ask what a word meant back then, not only what it means now. They read the Bible beside other old writings, like the Ugarit tablets and 1 Enoch. This helps them hear a text the way its first readers may have heard it.

words.d: the old lands of Egypt, Israel, Syria, Iraq and nearby places, long ago
the people who first heard or read a text in their own time and place

look.title: A Note From Long Ago
look.text: Imagine someone in the year 5000 finds a note that says: "Meet me by the L after school." In Chicago today, most people know the L is the city's train. A reader far in the future would not know that.
look.prompt: What would the future reader need to learn to understand the note? How is this like reading an old book like the Bible?

check.q: What is the ancient Near East?
choices: Old lands like Israel, Egypt, Syria and Iraq
check.why: The ancient Near East means the old lands of Egypt, Israel, Syria, Iraq and nearby places.

check.q: Why do researchers read the Bible beside other old writings?
choices: To learn what words meant to the first readers
check.why: Other old writings show ideas and words the first readers knew.

check.q: In the note from long ago, what would a future reader not know?
choices: That the L is Chicago's train
check.why: The L is a Chicago name a future reader would need to learn.

lessons.title: Checking a Claim Against the Text
lessons.mainIdea: A careful reader checks a big claim by finding the old text it points to and reading what it really says.
reading: Some books and videos make big claims about the Bible. One claim says that space aliens visited the ancient world. Another says giants built the pyramids. These claims often borrow old words from ancient texts.

Scholars read those same texts in their first languages. Heiser was one who wrote that the ancient-alien claims do not match what the texts say. Many other scholars agree. The claims often use words in ways the ancient writers never did.

You can check a *claim* too. First, ask where it comes from. Next, find the primary source it points to. Then read what the text says in its own context. A good reader looks at the *evidence* before deciding.

words.d: something a person says is true, which may or may not have evidence
facts or texts that help show whether a claim fits

look.title: Check the Claim
look.text: A video says: "An old text proves aliens built a city." A careful reader asks three questions. Which text? What does it actually say? What did the words mean to the people who wrote them?
look.prompt: Pick one of the three questions. Why does it help you check the claim?

check.q: What did Heiser and many other scholars say about ancient-alien claims?
choices: They come from the Book of Psalms
They do not match what the ancient texts say
check.why: Heiser and many scholars found that these claims do not fit the texts.

check.q: What is a good first step to check a claim?
choices: Believe it if it sounds exciting
Ask where the claim comes from
check.why: The reading says to begin by asking where a claim comes from.

check.q: What does evidence mean?
choices: Facts or texts that help show whether a claim fits
check.why: Evidence is the facts or texts used to test a claim.

review.q: Which of these is a primary source?
review.why: The Great Isaiah Scroll is an old hand-made copy of Isaiah, so it is a primary source.

review.q: What do we call a copy of a text written by hand?
review.why: A manuscript is a hand-written copy.

review.q: What were the Bible's three first languages?
review.why: The Hebrew Bible is mostly Hebrew with some Aramaic; the New Testament is in Greek.

review.q: Where was the Septuagint translation begun?
review.why: Jewish scholars in Alexandria began the Greek translation in the 200s BCE.

review.q: What do the Ugarit tablets show that helps scholars read Psalm 82?
choices: A council of gods led by El
review.why: The tablets describe El's assembly, which scholars compare with the council in Psalm 82.

review.q: Which scholar studied the Book of Giants scroll from Qumran in 1997?
review.why: Loren Stuckenbruck published The Book of Giants from Qumran in 1997.

review.q: Why does elohim need context to be understood?
choices: It can mean one God or many beings
review.why: Elohim can mean Israel's God or other beings; the words around it show which.

review.q: In the story, what did Nina's teacher tell her to read first?
choices: The psalm itself, her primary source
review.why: The teacher said to start with the psalm itself, then read the scholars.
